claims.claim: 4-tier extensibility hierarchy in Claude Code: MCP (external tools) / Skills (instructions + resources) / Subagents (isolated task runners) / Hooks (lifecycle triggers). Each tier solves different problem.
claims.evidence: Official docs architecture overview; community consensus (Dean Blank mental model March 2026).

claims.claim: MCP is for external tool/data integration (API calls, DB queries, external services); Skills is for reusable instruction patterns; Subagents is for context isolation; Hooks is for event-triggered automation.
claims.evidence: Official MCP docs + skills docs + subagents docs + hooks docs mapping.

claims.claim: Decision tree for selection: (1) Do I need external state/API? -> MCP. (2) Reusable prompt logic? -> Skill. (3) Context isolation needed? -> Subagent. (4) Lifecycle event hook? -> Hook.
claims.evidence: Derived from official docs; simplified from community decision trees.

claims.claim: Skills + Hooks overlap: can implement auto-triggered workflows (e.g., pre-commit quality check). Difference: Hook is OS-level event, Skill auto-invoke is LLM-decided.
claims.evidence: Hooks docs + skill paths field overlap analysis.

claims.claim: Skills + Subagents overlap: skill with context:fork becomes de-facto subagent invocation; difference is skill provides instructions while subagent provides environment.
claims.evidence: R1.C16 + docs subagent-vs-skill comparison.

claims.claim: Skills + MCP overlap: skill with allowed-tools: [mcp-server__tool] can bundle MCP invocation. Difference: MCP is data layer, skill with MCP is workflow wrapping data layer.
claims.evidence: Community hybrid pattern examples.

claims.claim: Token economics by tier (for 100 invocations, approximate): Skills ~$4.80-90 depending on model (Haiku-Opus); Subagent adds ~$2 per invocation for context-fork overhead; MCP call adds API fees not tokens.
claims.evidence: Derived from Anthropic pricing + skill size assumptions.

claims.claim: Model routing via skill model: field enables per-skill cost optimization: Haiku for simple tasks, Sonnet default, Opus for complex synthesis.
claims.evidence: R2.C9 model field + community cost optimization patterns.

claims.claim: Use case -> tier mapping examples: GitHub PR review (Skill for logic + MCP for GH API + Subagent for isolated review), Deploy pipeline (Hook pre-commit + Skill for deploy steps), Research gathering (Subagent fan-out with shared skill).
claims.evidence: Community patterns + Anthropic official plugin examples.

claims.claim: Decision matrix priorities: start with Skills (lowest overhead) -> escalate to Subagent for context isolation -> add MCP only for external integration -> add Hook only for lifecycle automation. Prefer simplest tier that solves the problem.
claims.evidence: Community best-practices consensus.

claims.claim: Commands (Claude Code 2.1+ merged with skills) are a UX-level abstraction, not a distinct tier; a command is a slash-invocable skill.
claims.evidence: R1.C3 merge + R3.C5.

claims.claim: Maciej's system analysis: 35 skills are agent definitions (individual roles), 42 commands are orchestrator skills that invoke preset ensembles. Architecturally: orchestrator-skill pattern at command layer + agent-skill pattern at skill layer.
claims.evidence: Project CLAUDE.md + generate_skills.js + generate_commands.js.

claims.claim: Cost optimization: Haiku for extractor roles (R5's Deep Research v2 uses Haiku for E1-E7 extracts), Sonnet for researcher roles, Opus for orchestrator/critic/synthesis.
claims.evidence: Maciej's /deep-research-v2 preset routing spec.

claims.claim: Subagent with skills preload field: enables skills to be loaded into subagent system prompt at startup (vs lazy on-invoke in main session). Rationale: subagent has short lifespan, no time for lazy load.
claims.evidence: R1.C10 subagent-vs-skill table (skills field).

claims.claim: Anti-pattern: using MCP where skill suffices. Example: wrapping a pure text transformation as MCP server adds I/O overhead + deployment complexity when a skill could do it in context.
claims.evidence: Community anti-pattern reports.

claims.claim: Anti-pattern: subagent for simple lookups. context:fork has startup cost (~2k tokens); not justified for 1-shot queries that fit in main context.
claims.evidence: R5.C7 cost breakdown + community perf reports.

claims.claim: Scoping decision: Skills at Personal scope for user-wide reuse (Maciej's 35), Project scope for team conventions, Plugin scope for shareable distribution.
claims.evidence: R1.C1 scope priority + plugin distribution rationale.

claims.claim: Hooks run OUTSIDE Claude reasoning (pre/post tool use, pre/post edit, etc.) and can gate or augment skill execution; useful for policy enforcement.
claims.evidence: Hooks docs events + policy use case.

claims.claim: Subagent lifespan: one-shot (ephemeral) by default; stateful multi-turn subagent requires explicit design. Context fork does not persist state beyond the single invocation.
claims.evidence: Subagent docs lifecycle section.

claims.claim: When all four tiers combine: complex workflows use Hook (trigger) -> Skill (orchestrator) -> Subagent (isolated task) -> MCP (external data). This is the 'full-stack' agent architecture pattern.
claims.evidence: Community advanced patterns + Anthropic enterprise use cases.

conflicts_flagged.description: Skill with context:fork blurs line between Skill and Subagent; some community guides treat them as same tier, others as distinct. Documentation ambiguity.
Cost trade-off: Opus orchestrator with Haiku workers saves money but coordination complexity rises; Sonnet-only is simpler but 5x more expensive. No consensus on sweet spot.

gaps_flagged.description: No official benchmark comparing 4-tier hybrid vs skill-only workflow for same task (e.g., end-to-end PR review).
Interaction of Hook triggering Skill with context:fork: does fork isolation apply? Empirical test needed.

summary: R5 systematizes the 4-tier hierarchy (MCP/Skills/Subagents/Hooks) with decision tree, overlap zones with hybrid examples, token economics breakdown, and maps Maciej's system (35 skills = agent defs, 42 commands = orchestrators). Core principle: start with simplest tier.
